items.stem: During development, how does Vite serve your application modules?

options.text: Over native ES modules, transforming files on demand without bundling the whole app
options.rationale: Correct: Vite serves source as native ESM for fast startup and HMR.

options.text: By bundling the entire app with Rollup on every change
options.rationale: Full bundling on each change is what Vite avoids in dev.

options.text: By precompiling to a single CommonJS file
options.rationale: Vite dev uses ESM, not a CommonJS bundle.

options.text: By running everything through Babel in the browser
options.rationale: Vite uses esbuild/native ESM, not in-browser Babel.

items.explanation: Correct: Vite serves source as native ESM for fast startup and HMR.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about Vite production builds are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Production builds are bundled with Rollup
options.rationale: Correct: Vite uses Rollup for optimised production output.

options.text: Content hashing in filenames enables long-term caching
options.rationale: Correct: hashed names bust caches only when content changes.

options.text: The dev server output is byte-identical to the production bundle
options.rationale: Dev and prod pipelines differ, so behaviour can diverge.

options.text: Code splitting is impossible in Vite
options.rationale: Rollup supports code splitting and dynamic imports.

items.explanation: Correct: Vite uses Rollup for optimised production output.

items.stem: In Vite, which environment variables are exposed to client code?

options.rationale: Correct: Vite only exposes VITE_-prefixed vars to the client to avoid leaking secrets.
Unprefixed vars stay server/build-only and are not exposed.
There is no SECRET_ convention; the prefix is VITE_.

options.text: None; Vite never exposes env vars

items.explanation: Correct: Vite only exposes VITE_-prefixed vars to the client to avoid leaking secrets.
